title: DevOps Fundamentals
summary: Learn DevOps culture and practice: version control and branching, CI/CD pipelines, containers with Docker, infrastructure as code, monitoring, SLOs and error budgets, and the metrics that measure delivery.
audience: Developers, system administrators, IT students and cloud learners

body.p: DevOps is a way of working that brings software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops) together so teams can deliver changes quickly and reliably. Instead of developers "throwing code over the wall" to an operations team, one team shares responsibility for building, releasing and running the service.

list: Small, frequent changes are safer than big, rare releases: each change is easier to test, understand and undo.
Automate repetitive work: builds, tests, deployments and server setup.
Measure everything: performance, errors and how fast the team delivers.
Share knowledge and learn from failures without blame.
Build security in from the start (often called DevSecOps).

body.p: Code moves through a pipeline: commit to version control, automatic build and tests, packaging, deployment to a test environment, then to production, with monitoring feeding back into planning. Every step that a computer can do reliably is automated.

body.tip: DevOps is mostly about habits and collaboration; buying tools without changing how teams work achieves little.

body.p: Everything that defines a system belongs in version control (usually Git): application code, tests, configuration, pipeline definitions and infrastructure code. This gives a full history, makes changes reviewable and lets you rebuild any version.

list: Make small commits with clear messages explaining why.
Use short-lived branches and pull requests for review, merging back to the main branch often (trunk-based development).
Protect the main branch: require passing tests and a review before merging.
Tag releases so you know exactly what is running in production.
Never commit passwords or keys; use a secrets store and scan repositories for leaked secrets.

body.p: Long-lived branches drift apart and cause painful merges. Feature flags let unfinished features be merged but kept switched off until ready.

body.tip: If a change is too big to review in 20 minutes, split it into smaller pull requests.

body.p: Continuous integration (CI) means every change is automatically built and tested when pushed, so problems are found within minutes. Continuous delivery (CD) keeps the software always releasable, with automated deployment to test environments; continuous deployment goes further and releases every passing change to production automatically.

body.code:
name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest

body.p: On every push or pull request, this workflow checks out the code, installs Python and the dependencies, and runs the tests. A failing test blocks the merge.

list: Run fast unit tests first, then slower integration tests.
Deploy the same built package to every environment.
Use blue-green or canary releases: send a small share of traffic to the new version first.
Make rollback quick and practised.

body.tip: Keep the pipeline fast. If it takes an hour, people stop waiting for it and bugs slip through.

body.p: A container packages an application with everything it needs to run (libraries, runtime and settings) so it behaves the same on a laptop, a test server and the cloud. Containers share the host's operating-system kernel, so they start in seconds and use far less memory than full virtual machines.

body.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

body.p: Each line builds a layer: start from a small Python image, set the working folder, install dependencies, copy the code, document the port and set the start command. Copying requirements.txt before the rest of the code lets Docker reuse the dependency layer when only code changes, which speeds up builds.

list: docker build -t myapp:1.0 . builds an image.
docker run -p 8000:8000 myapp:1.0 runs it as a container.
Images are stored in registries; orchestrators such as Kubernetes run many containers across many servers, restarting failed ones and scaling them.

body.tip: Use small, official base images, keep them updated, and do not run containers as root unless you must.

body.p: Infrastructure as code (IaC) describes servers, networks, databases and permissions in text files that tools turn into real resources. Tools include Terraform and OpenTofu, cloud-provider templates, and configuration tools such as Ansible.

list: Repeatable: build identical test and production environments.
Reviewable: infrastructure changes go through pull requests like code.
Recoverable: rebuild after a disaster from the definitions.
Documented: the files show exactly what exists and why.

body.p: Prefer immutable infrastructure: instead of logging in to patch a running server by hand, build a new image or container with the change and replace the old one. Manual changes create "snowflake" servers that nobody can reproduce.
Keep environment-specific values (database addresses, feature switches) in configuration, and secrets in a secrets manager, not in code.

body.tip: Run IaC in "plan" mode first to see exactly what will be created, changed or destroyed before applying it.

body.p: You cannot run what you cannot see. Observability combines metrics (numbers over time such as request rate, errors and latency), logs (detailed event records) and traces (the path of one request through many services). Alerts should fire on symptoms users feel, not on every small blip.

Site reliability engineering (SRE) sets service level objectives (SLOs), such as 99.9% of requests succeeding over 30 days. The remaining 0.1% is an error budget: for availability, 30 x 24 x 60 x 0.001 = 43.2 minutes of downtime a month. While budget remains, the team ships features; if it is spent, the team focuses on reliability.

list: Deployment frequency: how often you release.
Lead time for changes: from commit to production.
Change failure rate: if 3 of 40 deployments caused incidents, 3 / 40 = 7.5%.
Time to restore service: if three incidents took 25, 35 and 60 minutes, the mean is 40 minutes.

body.p: After incidents, hold blameless post-mortems that focus on how the system allowed the failure and what will prevent a repeat.

body.tip: Start with the four golden signals for each service: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.

quiz.q: What is the main aim of DevOps?
options: Delivering changes quickly and reliably through shared ownership and automation

quiz.q: Why are small, frequent releases safer?
options: Each change is easier to test, understand and undo

quiz.q: Which should NOT be committed to a Git repository?

options: Automatically building and testing every change

quiz.q: In the example workflow, what runs the tests?

options: Sends a small share of traffic to the new version first

quiz.q: Why copy requirements.txt before the rest of the code in a Dockerfile?
options: So the dependency layer is reused when only code changes
Each need a full operating system
Share the host kernel and start faster

quiz.q: What does infrastructure as code provide?
options: Repeatable, reviewable infrastructure from text definitions
A server changed by hand that nobody can reproduce

quiz.q: A 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days allows about how much downtime?
3 of 40 deployments caused incidents. What is the change failure rate?
Incidents took 25, 35 and 60 minutes to restore. The mean time to restore is:

options: How the system allowed the failure and how to prevent it
